newsitem.title: UK: BT to be hit by 500 mln stg of utility tax.
newsitem.headline: BT to be hit by 500 mln stg of utility tax.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc said on Wednesday it expected the government to impose a utility tax in the order of 500 million pounds ($829.6 million) spread over two years on it.
But the telecoms giant declined to say whether it would mount a legal challenge to the levy, which some analysts had expected to be nearer 1.0 billion pounds.
"Whilst not a small sum, it is considerably lower than earlier speculation might have expected," a company spokesman told Reuters.
"The Chancellor (finance minister) does appear to have taken account of the special characteristics of BT in determining the formula for devising the tax.
"This will no doubt help the BT board when it decides how to proceed once the finance bill has been published."

However, BT's chairman Sir Iain Vallance said in a statement that any retrospective tax was a bad tax and the company was disappointed to have been caught up in a levy he said was a "tax on success not on excess".

"We fully support the government's welfare-to-work programme. But we see no justification for taxing BT in this way when the company has made no excess returns and is neither a monopoly nor a utility.
"Indeed, uniquely amongst the privatised comapnies, its return to taxpayers since privatisation have been greater than its returns to shareholders," he added.
Analysts said earlier they expected BT to benefit by around 70 million pounds per year from a two percentage point cut of corporation tax to 31 percent.

They do not expect the company to mount a legal challenge to the windfall levy, despite BT's threats in May, when Vallance said the company would be "failing in our fiduciary duty to shareholders" not to challenge it.

"If we are stung in a big way for this tax and if it can be challenged legally, we owe it to our shareholders to challenge it," Vallance said after the company reported annual pretax profits of 3.2 billion pounds.

Earlier on Wednesday, British Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown unveiled his budget in which he said he planned to raise a total of 5.2 billion pounds from a windfall tax on electricity companies, water groups, airports authority BAA Plc, former British Gas firms, BT and Railtrack Plc.
The tax is in two instalments, the first on December 1, 1997 and the second a year later.

The Inland Revenue said the levy would be charged at a rate of 23 percent on the difference between company value at the time of flotation and company value calculated by reference to profits over a four-year period after privatisations.
The Labour Government, which swept to power in a landslide election victory on May 1, plans to use the tax to pay for welfare programme to get the young and long-term unemployed back to work.

The government devised the tax after outrage at what it calls the "excess profits" of privatised utilities, whose large executive salaries and surging dividends have angered consumer groups and parliamentarians.
